subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: Liam stared at the equation on the kitchen table in Leeds, ten minutes before his older sister Olga would check his homework. He changed a plus to a minus. Wrong. He swapped two numbers, divided everything by two, erased the second line and started over. Suddenly the answer matched the one at the back of the book. He grinned, then looked at the page and realised he had no idea which change had done it. Olga glanced over. "Nice. How did you get it?" Liam opened his mouth and closed it. "I just changed stuff until it worked," he said. The next problem looked exactly as impossible as the first.

qa.q: What did Liam change first when he began?
qa.a: Liam changed a plus to a minus.

qa.q: What was Liam feeling when Olga asked how he got the answer?
qa.a: Liam felt caught out and unsure, because he opened his mouth and closed it, knowing he could not say which change had worked.

qa.q: What could Liam do differently on the next problem?
qa.a: He could change one thing at a time and write down what each change did, so he can say why an answer works.

qa.q: How might Olga see Liam's matching answer?
qa.a: Olga may be pleased at first, then notice that a correct answer alone does not show understanding, which is why she asks how he got it.

grounding: Shows a teenager changing things at random on a maths problem and being unable to say what worked.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: In the school computer lab, Gurleen's program printed nothing. She deleted a bracket, retyped a line, renamed a variable and changed 10 to 100. Still nothing. The bell for the end of lab was minutes away and her hands were fast and sweaty. She commented out half the code, brought it back, then pasted a line from the next screen. Numbers suddenly scrolled down. Arnab sir came by. "What fixed it?" Gurleen stared at the screen. "I don't know, sir. Maybe the bracket?" She could not say. He asked her to undo the changes and look at the first error message she had scrolled past. She read it slowly, for the first time.

qa.q: What did Gurleen change 10 to?
qa.a: Gurleen changed 10 to 100.

qa.q: What might Gurleen be worried about as the bell gets closer?
qa.a: She is worried about running out of time and having nothing working, and the panic makes her hands fast and her changes wild.

qa.q: What could Gurleen try instead of changing things at random?
qa.a: She could read the first error message first, then change one thing at a time and check the result each time.

qa.q: What is it like for Arnab sir to see Gurleen produce numbers she cannot explain?
qa.a: Arnab sir sees the program run but knows nothing has been learned, so he asks what fixed it and guides her back to the error message.

grounding: Shows a teenager making frantic random changes to a bug and being unable to say what fixed it.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage:
Thomas: "Nilesh, why is your game crashing?"
Nilesh: "No idea. I've been trying stuff."
Thomas: "What stuff?"
Nilesh: "I changed the speed, deleted that loop, put it back, renamed some variables, copied a line from a video."
Thomas: "And now?"
Nilesh: "Now it crashes at a different place. Or maybe the same place. I don't know."
Thomas: "What did the error say the first time?"
Nilesh: "Didn't read it. I panicked. The demo's at school tomorrow."
Thomas: "Okay. Undo everything back to this morning."
Nilesh: "Everything?!"
Thomas: "Yes. Then run it, read the error, and change one thing."
Nilesh: (after ten minutes) "It says 'list index out of range' on line 58."
Thomas: "See? Now we have a clue."

qa.q: What error did Nilesh finally read?
qa.a: 'List index out of range' on line 58.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling while changing things at random?
qa.a: Nilesh felt panicked about the demo tomorrow, so trying anything felt better than stopping to think.

qa.q: What did Thomas suggest, and why does it work better?
qa.a: Undo everything, read the error and change one thing, which turns random guessing into clues you can learn from.

qa.q: How might Thomas feel hearing Nilesh's list of changes?
qa.a: Thomas might feel a bit amused and worried, seeing that the random changes had left Nilesh more lost than before.

grounding: A dialogue shows a teenager making random changes to a buggy game in a panic and not knowing what fixed or broke it.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: I'm Jahnavi, and in Class Ten I had a way of doing maths that my friend Preeti called "throwing darts". When a question stumped me in a test, I'd panic. I'd add the numbers, then multiply them, then try a formula from the last chapter, then divide by two, hoping something looked like an answer. Sometimes I got it right. But afterwards, when Preeti asked how I solved it, I honestly couldn't say. I'd learned nothing. In the pre-boards, I threw darts at five questions and got one. Preeti sat me down and made me write, before any calculation, what the question asked and what I knew. It felt slow. It worked.

qa.q: What did Preeti call Jahnavi's way of doing maths?
qa.a: Preeti called it "throwing darts".

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when a test question was a stumper?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt panicked, and trying anything seemed better than stopping to think.

qa.q: What did Preeti suggest, and why does it help?
qa.a: Writing what the question asked and what was known before calculating, so each step has a reason and can be learned from.

qa.q: How might Preeti see Jahnavi's lucky right answers?
qa.a: Preeti likely sees them as empty wins, since Jahnavi couldn't explain them and learned nothing.

grounding: A teenager recalls trying random operations in panic, sometimes getting lucky but never knowing what worked.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage:
Computer science teacher's note, Class 11, practical exam.
During today's practical, Disha's program stopped printing results. In the next twenty minutes, I watched her change the loop, delete a variable, add three print statements, rename the file and restart the computer twice. She was clearly panicking, typing fast and muttering. Her program ran by the end, but when I asked her what had fixed it, she said, "I don't know. Something." Her classmate Deepika, stuck on a similar error, had read the error message and fixed one line. In our next class, I will teach a short routine: read the error, guess why, change one thing, test.

qa.q: How many times did Disha restart the computer?
qa.a: She restarted the computer twice.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling during the twenty minutes?
qa.a: She was panicking, typing fast and muttering, anxious to make the program work somehow.

qa.q: What routine will the teacher teach, and why?
qa.a: Read the error, guess why, change one thing, test, so students learn what actually fixes a problem.

qa.q: How does Deepika's approach compare to Disha's, from the teacher's view?
qa.a: The teacher sees Deepika's calm reading of the error as far more useful, since Deepika fixed one line and knew why.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager making random changes under exam pressure and not knowing what fixed the bug.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage:
Friday
The LED circuit for the physics project finally lit up at 9:40 pm, and I have no idea why.
It wouldn't glow all evening. I panicked and started changing everything: flipped the LED, swapped the red and black wires, moved the resistor two holes down, borrowed Papa's new battery, pressed everything harder into the board. Somewhere in there it came on. I screamed and Papa came running.
Kamal, my lab partner, texted: "What was wrong?" I typed "fixed it!!" and then just sat there. Fixed WHAT? I changed about eight things at once and didn't write any of them down.
Now I'm scared to even touch it in case it goes off again before Monday's demo. Not really the feeling you want after "fixing" something. 😬
Mahima

qa.q: What time did the LED circuit finally light up?
qa.a: At 9:40 pm.

qa.q: How does Mahima feel after the circuit lights up?
qa.a: Mahima is relieved at first but then uneasy and scared, not knowing which change worked or whether it will fail before the demo.

qa.q: What could Mahima try next time the circuit won't work?
qa.a: Change one thing at a time, test after each change, and jot it down, so the fix is known and can be repeated at the demo.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel if the circuit fails again at Monday's demo?
qa.a: As lab partner, Kamal would likely be worried and let down after the cheerful "fixed it!!", with nothing to go on to fix it quickly.

grounding: Shows a teenager who panics over a faulty circuit, changes many things at random and cannot tell what fixed it, so nothing is learned.
